title: House Robber
keyIdea: At each house: rob it and jump to i + 2, or skip it and go to i + 1. best(i) = max(nums[i] + best(i + 2), best(i + 1)). Fill from the right; only the next two values are ever needed, so two variables are enough.

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: Try both choices at every house with no saving: rob (index + 2) or skip (index + 1).
approaches.why: Each call branches into two, and the same index is solved again and again (like Fibonacci). The stack is at most n deep.
approaches.warn: Too slow for n = 100: the same subproblems are recomputed exponentially many times.

approaches.name: Memoization (last house as base)
approaches.idea: Your commented version: stop at the last house and return nums[index]; only call index + 2 when that house exists (tempAns stays 0 otherwise). Save each answer in dp.
approaches.why: Each index is computed once and then read from dp; dp and the recursion stack are O(n).

approaches.name: Memoization
approaches.idea: Same recursion, but save best(index) in dp the first time; base case: index past the end → 0.
approaches.why: Each index 0..n − 1 is computed once (2 calls each), everything else is a dp lookup. dp array plus recursion stack: O(n).

approaches.name: Tabulation
approaches.idea: dp of size n + 2 with dp[n] = dp[n + 1] = 0; fill i from n − 1 down to 0 with dp[i] = max(nums[i] + dp[i + 2], dp[i + 1]); answer dp[0].
approaches.why: One loop over the houses; the dp array has n + 2 entries.

approaches.name: Two variables
approaches.idea: Your active code: the tabulation keeping only next1 = best(i + 1) and next2 = best(i + 2). curr = max(nums[i] + next2, next1), then shift.
approaches.why: One pass over the houses; only two numbers are stored.

options: dp[i] only reads dp[i + 1] and dp[i + 2]
